What happens to bank accounts when someone dies? (Australia)

By the Afterkeep research team · Reviewed on 26 Oct 2026

Once you tell an Australian bank about a death, it secures accounts in the person's sole name: online banking is switched off and debits are restricted. Joint account holders can usually keep using joint accounts. Under the Banking Code of Practice, banks act on a valid executor or next-of-kin instruction within 14 business days and can release money for funeral costs before probate.

Key facts

  • Sole accounts secured once the bank is told
  • Joint accounts usually continue
  • Instructions actioned within 14 business days
  • Funeral costs payable before probate

What are the steps?

  1. Tell each bank as soon as practicable: online, by phone, in a branch, or through the Australian Death Notification Service once a death certificate exists.
  2. Expect sole-name accounts to be secured. Internet and app banking logins are removed, cards are cancelled and debits are restricted. Direct credits can still arrive.
  3. Find recurring payments. CommBank says it can give the estate representative a list of regular payments on the deceased's debit card and copies of statements; ask your bank for the same. Cancel subscriptions with each provider.
  4. Prove you can act. Banks usually want your ID plus a verified copy of the will (executor) or the death certificate naming you as next of kin.
  5. Need money for the funeral? Before probate, a representative can ask the bank to pay or reimburse funeral costs or probate filing fees, with an invoice or receipt.
  6. Ask whether a grant is needed. Each bank decides; NAB lists a $100,000 total-in-credit threshold among the cases where it needs a Grant of Representation.
  7. With the bank's documents in hand, sign its forms to close accounts and release funds. You can open a deceased estate account if the bank offers one.
  8. Planning ahead: list your banks and accounts (not passwords) in your estate inventory, and tell your executor where it is.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use a joint account after my partner dies?

Usually yes. The Banking Code says a joint account holder may keep operating the account under its terms, and CommBank and NAB say joint accounts in credit continue.

How long do banks take to act?

Under the Banking Code, once verified documents are received, banks act on a valid estate representative's instruction within 14 business days. Finalising an estate can take weeks to months; CommBank says a couple of weeks to a few months.

Can the bank pay for the funeral before probate?

Yes. The Banking Code lets a representative ask for funds to pay or reimburse funeral expenses or probate filing fees, with proof of the invoice or receipt. NAB covers these up to $15,000.

Will direct debits keep coming out?

Banks restrict debits on sole accounts once notified, but some card payments may still go through. Check statements and cancel each subscription with the provider.

Can I use their online banking to pay bills?

No. Banks remove the deceased's internet and app banking logins after notification. Pay bills through the estate process instead.

Do I need probate to close a bank account?

Not always. The bank tells you if it needs a Grant of Probate or Letters of Administration; if not, it explains how to finalise the estate.
